82356973.extract:
Mugging, also known as personal robbery or street robbery, is a form of robbery and street crime that occurs in public places, often in urban areas, particularly at night. It involves the use of force or the threat of force to take property from a victim. Muggings can vary in severity, ranging from minor thefts to violent assaults. The legal consequences of mugging can be severe, with imprisonment and fines being common outcomes. This article will explore the various aspects of mugging, including its definition, types, legal implications, and notable cases.

Types of mugging can include purse snatching, where a perpetrator quickly takes a victim's purse or bag; wallet theft, where a perpetrator steals a victim's wallet or other small valuables; and violent muggings, where a perpetrator uses or threatens to use physical force to take property. Muggings often occur in areas with high foot traffic, such as streets, parks, and public transportation, but can also happen in quieter areas, especially at night.

The legal implications of mugging can be significant. In many jurisdictions, mugging is treated as a felony, and the penalties can include imprisonment, fines, and probation. The severity of the punishment depends on the specific circumstances of the crime, such as whether a weapon was involved or if the victim was injured. Self-defense can be a legal justification for the use of force by the victim, but the extent of the force used must be proportionate to the threat faced.

Notable mugging cases include the Brink's robbery in Boston, where a group of men in masks robbed a bank in 1950, setting off a massive search for the perpetrators. Another significant case is the Hatton Garden robbery in London in 2015, where a group of thieves broke into a diamond vault and stole over £23 million in diamonds and precious metals.

Statistics on mugging vary by location and year, but in the United States, the FBI reported an estimated 267,988 robberies nationwide in 2019, with the robbery rate of 81.6 per 100,000 inhabitants. The vast majority of individuals sentenced for robbery were men, with nearly 70% being Black or Hispanic. The legal and social implications of mugging highlight the importance of community safety and crime prevention measures.

mugging
=======

The act of physical attack upon an isolated pedestrian on a public street at night and the taking of money and effects from his person. While generally not a crime on its own, a mugger may be criminally liable for the [felony](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/felony) of common-law [robbery](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/robbery). See[_State v. Smith_](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1955849/state-v-smith/). Mugging can also connote a physical attack on a pedestrian from behind. See also:[_Goldberg v. National Life Ins. Co._](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/774/559/9885/)

In a gang context, “mean mugging” is a gang term for challenging down a rival gang member by staring them down, and is often a precursor to more serious violence. See[_Saechao v. Brazelton_](https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/5914f296add7b0493497f8fb).

[](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)What is Mugging?
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Mugging is a criminal offense which involves a threatened or actual physical attack with the intent to rob an individual. Mugging is also known as [robbery](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/robbery-lawyers.html).

It is normally a street crime that is carried out by petty thieves.

Contents

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)What is Robbery?

Robbery is a form of felony theft. It is defined as the taking of property from another individual by the use of:

*   Force;
*   Intimidation; or
*   The threat of force.

Because of this, robbery is sometimes referred to as larceny by threat of force. In some states, the use or threat of force does not have to be directed at the intended victim or victims.

The threat, however, must be immediate and the crime must have been committed in the presence of the victim. If a robbery is committed with the use of a firearm or another type of [deadly weapon](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/what-constitutes-a-deadly-weapon.html), it may be considered armed robbery.

A conviction of armed robbery will result in harsher penalties for a defendant. Although the laws may vary slightly in each state regarding the exact definition of what conduct constitutes a robbery, the general elements of robbery typically include:

*   The taking and carrying away;
*   Of the personal property of another;
*   From their possession or in their presence;
*   Against their will;
*   By: 
    *   force;
    *   fear;
    *   violence;
    *   intimidation; or
    *   threat of force.

It is important to note that, although the terms burglary and robbery are often used interchangeably, they are not the same criminal offense. [Burglary](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/penalties-and-sentencing-for-burglary.html) is the breaking and entering into a dwelling place or other building with the intent to commit a felony therein.

One of the main differences between the two is that a burglary includes breaking and entering and does not require the use of force.

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)What is a Holdup Robbery?

A holdup robbery is a certain type of robbery that is committed with the use of a deadly or dangerous weapon. In some cases, it may also be referred to as a stick up.

The term stick up originated with the common command used by a robber to their victim to stick or hold up their hands in the air so they will not be able to defend themselves. The weapons that are commonly used include knives and guns.

Holdup robberies may occur under many different circumstances. This type of crime, however, is most commonly associated with victims such as:

*   Pedestrians. Because they are walking down a street, they may be easy targets, especially in areas where there are not many other people around;
*   Passengers in a vehicle or public transportation;
*   Individuals who are likely to have case on hand to rob, including: 
    *   retail store clerks;
    *   bankers; and
    *   cashiers;

*   Bankers;
*   Cashiers; and
*   Cargo transport workers as they often possess valuable items that a robber will target.

The criminal offense of robbery may also be defined as a theft in addition to the use of force or an assault. In many cases, when a holdup robbery is committed the force used will involve the threat of harm from a weapon such as a gun or a knife.

In certain cases, the robber only has to pretend that they possess a weapon in order to commit this offense. Because of this issue, the laws governing holdup robbers are commonly grouped in with the laws which govern [armed robbery](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/armed-robbery.html).

Armed robbery is a robbery charge which will result in more serious punishments if the defendant is convicted. Holdup robberies may include crimes which range from less serious to more serious.

These can include minor muggings to more serious crimes, such as bank robbery.

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)What if the Weapon was not Real?

In numerous jurisdictions, the laws are written to include the possibility that the weapon which is used in a holdup robbery was not real. Most of these laws treat the use of a [fake weapon for robbery](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/robbery-with-a-fake-weapon.html) just as the use of a real weapon in a holdup robbery, or armed robbery, would be treated.

If a victim is injured or killed, this will, of course, make a difference in the criminal sentence that the defendant will receive. Even if injury or death does not occur to the victim, however, the criminal offense of armed robbery is still committed.

If a victim believes that a robber does possess a gun, then they will respond according to the belief that they may be injured or killed if they do not comply with the demands of the robber. The victim will also be traumatized and the robber will still accomplish their goal of using intimidation and the victim’s fear to complete their crime.

Even if the threat was not genuine but the end result is the armed robbery being successful, then it will be treated as if it was an armed robbery. A robber may pretend that they have a gun by pressing some item into the victim’s back and pretending that the item is a gun.

In certain cases, a robber may modify a toy or some other object to resemble a real weapon.

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)What are Normal Sentences for Mugging?

It may be difficult to determine the length of a sentence for a criminal offense such as mugging because it is a crime which involves other offenses, such as assault and robbery. A mugger is often charged with armed robbery if they used a weapon.

If the perpetrator used a deadly weapon, they can be charged with aggravated robbery. If the incident occurred at or near a public road, the perpetrator may be charged with highway robbery.

These are all examples of felony charges which carry substantial prison time if the perpetrator is convicted. The possible consequences for a mugging include:

*   Imprisonment ranging from a year to life, depending on the facts of the case;
*   [Probation](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/violation-of-probation-lawyers.html);
*   Fines; and
*   Other consequences of a felony conviction.

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)What Should I do if I am Mugged?

If an individual is mugged, they should:

*   Immediately write down a description of the mugger for identity purposes;
*   Seek medical attention if needed;
*   File a police report immediately;
*   Cancel any credit cards that were stolen;
*   Contact their bank;
*   Contact their cell phone service provider;
*   Change their locks, if their keys were stolen; and
*   Learn from the experience.

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)Are there Any Defenses to Mugging?

Mugging is considered a serious criminal offense. The majority of defenses to mugging involve some form of an alibi, or a claim that the perpetrator is innocent because they could not have committed the offense.

A perpetrator may also claim that the robbery was committed against their will, for example, through [blackmail](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/blackmail.html) or other forms of duress. Another possible defense is that the victim gave consent to the taking of their property.

The defendant may also argue that the defendant was never placed into fear. It is important to note, however, that a defendant may still be held liable for a lesser-included offense, such as [larceny](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/felony-larceny.html).

Any defenses to robbery should be presented in a court of law.

### [](https://www.legalmatch.com/law-library/article/mugging.html)Should I Contact an Attorney?

If you have been charged with mugging, it is important to consult with a [criminal defense lawyer](https://www.legalmatch.com/criminal-lawyers.html). If you are convicted of a felony, it may alter many aspects of your life in addition to your criminal record.

Your attorney can review your case, determine what defenses may be available to you, and present those defenses on your behalf in court. In addition, your lawyer will appear with you whenever you attend a court proceeding.

=======

[Download Printable Document](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/topic-pages/robbery.pdf)****

### **Definition**

The FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program defines robbery as the taking or attempting to take anything of value from the care, custody, or control of a person or persons by force or threat of force or violence and/or by putting the victim in fear.

### **Overview**

*   There were an estimated 267,988 robberies nationwide in 2019. The estimated number of robberies decreased 4.7 percent from the 2018 estimate and decreased 18.3 percent from the 2015 estimate. The 2019 estimate was down 27.4 percent from the 2010 estimate.(See Tables **[1](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1)** and **[1A](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1/table-1a)**.)

*   The estimated robbery rate of 81.6 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2019 showed a decrease of 5.2 percent when compared with the 2018 rate.(See Tables **[1](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1)** and **[1A](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1/table-1a)**.)

*   In 2019, the average dollar value of property stolen per reported robbery was $1,797. Robberies accounted for an estimated $482 million in losses. Banks experienced the highest average dollar loss at $4,213 per offense.(Based on Tables **[1](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1)** and **[23](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-23)**.)

*   Among the robberies for which the UCR Program received weapon information in 2019, strong-arm tactics were used in 44.8 percent, firearms in 36.4 percent, and knives or cutting instruments in 8.5 percent. Other dangerous weapons were used in 10.3 percent of robberies in 2019.(Based on **[Table 19](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-19)**.)

### **Expanded data**

Expanded offense data are the details of the various offenses that the UCR Program collects beyond the count of how many crimes law enforcement agencies report. These details may include the type of weapon used in a crime, type or value of items stolen, and so forth. In addition, expanded data include trends (for example, 2-year comparisons) and rates per 100,000 inhabitants.

Expanded information regarding robbery is available in the following tables: ****

### **Robbery Location Figure**

This figure is a pie chart that shows the percentages of robbery offenses by location type in 2019. In the nation, 34.3 percent of robbery offenses occurred on streets or highways, 16.7 percent occurred at commercial houses, 15.8 percent occurred at residences, 6.6 percent occurred at convenience stores, 3.0 percent occurred at gas or service stations, 1.4 percent occurred at banks, and 22.2 percent occurred at miscellaneous locations.

**Mugging** (sometimes called **personal robbery** or **street robbery**) is a form of [robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbery "Robbery") and [street crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_crime "Street crime") that occurs in public places, often urban areas at night. It involves a [confrontation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confrontation "Confrontation") with a threat of violence. Muggers steal money or [personal property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_property "Personal property"), which is worth less than the payouts of commercial robbery but involves less time and planning. They may be motivated by money, [cultural capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_capital "Cultural capital"), or the thrill of the act. The risk of property loss, injury, or [psychological trauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_trauma "Psychological trauma") causes people to fear becoming victims of mugging.

The concept of mugging originated in 1940s United States, when [blackouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackout_(wartime) "Blackout (wartime)") of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") enabled committing crimes in the dark. It soon became the subject of [anti-Black racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Black_racism "Anti-Black racism"). In the United Kingdom, a media wave about mugging occurred in the 1970s, before which the concept had not been applied to British crimes. Police departments created "anti-mugging" units. The crime was often committed by [West Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indian "West Indian") youths, and there were widespread [racial stereotypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_stereotype "Racial stereotype") associating it with Black people. Some leftist criminologists said that the media inaccurately reported a [crime wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime "Crime") of mugging, including [Stuart Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Hall_(cultural_theorist) "Stuart Hall (cultural theorist)"), who called it a [moral panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_panic "Moral panic"). Political debate of mugging in the country peaked in the 1980s. In the 1990s, Brazilian media reported a mass mugging phenomenon known as _arrastão_, a term later used in Portugal.

Etymology and terminology
-------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mugging&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology and terminology")]

The word _[mug](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mug "wikt:mug")_ had several definitions in the nineteenth century. The noun _mugger_ had been used since the eighteenth century to refer to [earthenware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthenware "Earthenware") sellers before a [semantic shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantic_shift "Semantic shift") toward referring to thieves. The _[Dictionary of Americanisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John\_Russell\_Bartlett "John Russell Bartlett")_ documented the thief-related usage of the word among inmates at [Confederate prisons in the American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War_prison_camps "American Civil War prison camps").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamony1971130%E2%80%93131-1) The modern usage—referring to [robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbery "Robbery") against an individual, often by a group—originated in the 1940s among criminals and police.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeuneAlex1973260-2) The noun _mugging_ and the verb _mug_ entered British English from American English, becoming a [buzzword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzword "Buzzword") in late 1972 and early 1973.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawson1972306-3)

_Mugging_ is a common term for personal robbery,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012202-4) though personal robbery also encompasses forms of theft such as [carjacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carjacking "Carjacking").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEW%C3%BCllenweberBurrell20235-5) Other terms for personal robbery include _snatch theft_ and _street robbery_, as it is an example of a [street crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_crime "Street crime").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPorter2010535-6) The terms _mugging_, _street robbery_, and _street crime_ are often interchangeable, though usage varies.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStockdale19981-7)

Mugging is a form of [robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbery "Robbery"). Mugging itself is generally not a criminal offense; perpetrators of the act commit the crime of robbery, though mugging is a more specific concept.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-LII-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWykes2007164-9) Unlike other forms of robbery, mugging is a [personal offense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_law#Personal_offenses "Criminal law"). It typically involves less planning and smaller payouts than commercial robbery,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012202-4) and it is usually committed by inexperienced criminals who rely on fear.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012203-10)

Mugging often involves an attack on a victim walking alone at night.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-LII-8) Perpetrators steal money or valuable [personal property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_property "Personal property") such as [cell phones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_phone "Cell phone").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012202-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-LII-8) Actual or threatened violence is a major aspect of mugging, which often uses weapons such as [knives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knives "Knives").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012202Lejeune1977123-11) The level of violence can vary, with some muggings resulting in injury or death. The level of violence and the emotional response contribute to a victim's level of crisis.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeeRosenthal1983598-12) Victims often face loss of property, injury, or fear, and they may gain [psychological trauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_trauma "Psychological trauma").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012203-10) The possibility of such outcomes results in a widespread fear of mugging.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeune1977123-13)

[Motives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motive_(law) "Motive (law)") for mugging include need for money, desire to increase [social status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_status "Social status"), and the thrill of the act.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012203Lejeune1977124-14) The latter two motives are common among younger people, while the need for money often motivates habitual drug users to commit street robbery.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeakinSmithsonSpencerMedina-Ariza200754-15) Though mugging takes more time than other crimes and brings little money, perpetrators are motivated by a feeling of power.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTESandbergPedersen2011130-16) Compared to commercial robbery, street robbery is a more reliable source of money due to its speed, simplicity, and low punishment rate; this is motivating for people who lack legitimate sources of money.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHardingDeucharDensleyMcLean2019880-17) Muggers are often motivated by [peer pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_pressure "Peer pressure"), which [normalizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalization_(sociology) "Normalization (sociology)") the behavior.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeune1977132%E2%80%93133-18) People involved in [street gangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_gang "Street gang") gain [cultural capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_capital "Cultural capital") from it.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHardingDeucharDensleyMcLean2019884-19)

Street robbery usually occurs in urban areas.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithFrazeeDavison2000497-20) It is often associated with night,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEW%C3%BCllenweberBurrell20234%E2%80%935-21) though it frequently occurs at other times of day.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeakinSmithsonSpencerMedina-Ariza200756-22) Muggers usually work within small, familiar areas, such as the surroundings of their homes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernascoBlockRuiter2012136BurrellBullBond2012204,_215Lejeune1977135SmithFrazeeDavison2000496,_503-23) Street robberies occur within a few [city blocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_block "City block") of places that are likely to have cash, like stores, bars, illegal businesses, or [ATMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATM "ATM").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBernascoBlockRuiter2012119%E2%80%93120,_123,_135-24) Incidents are often clustered at points within cities such as [bus stops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_stop "Bus stop").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHartMiethe2014190LiuLanEckKang20201%E2%80%932-25) Many incidents occur in places with activity in the [night-time economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night-time_economy "Night-time economy"); such cases frequently involve [alcohol intoxication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_intoxication "Alcohol intoxication") or violence.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEW%C3%BCllenweberBurrell20236,_10-26) Street robbers sometimes target other criminals opportunistically; such cases are less commonly reported to police.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeakinSmithsonSpencerMedina-Ariza200758-27)

A mugging typically lasts a few minutes.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeune1977127-28) It begins with the perpetrator [assessing the risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_assessment "Risk assessment") of conducting the act.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeune1977127-28) Muggers select victims whom they perceive as vulnerable or likely to have money.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeune1977134-29) They may initiate a [confrontation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confrontation "Confrontation") by feigning a non-threatening encounter.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeakinSmithsonSpencerMedina-Ariza200761Lejeune1977136%E2%80%93139LejeuneAlex1973266-30) The confrontation occurs in a short range, enabling personal contact, such as shoving, that may surprise the victim.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeuneAlex1973260-2) The perpetrator may display weapons or implicitly threaten violence.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeakinSmithsonSpencerMedina-Ariza200762-31) They attempt to take control of the victim, which creates an unpredictable situation for both parties based on their perceptions of each other.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeune1977136%E2%80%93139-32) Though muggers usually do not desire to induce violence, confrontations often become violent when they lose control or perceive resistance.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeakinSmithsonSpencerMedina-Ariza200763Lejeune1977141%E2%80%93143-33)

The concept of mugging originated in the United States in the 1940s.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoran2008203-34)[Blackouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackout_(wartime) "Blackout (wartime)") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") enabled people to commit crimes in the dark, inciting the popularity of muggings in cities such as [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamony1971131-35) Mugging narratives were [racialized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racialized "Racialized") since the origin of the concept,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEsteves2012136-36) and, in the post-war era, media in New York City associated mugging with [the Black population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans_in_New_York_City "African Americans in New York City"). African-American communist politician [Benjamin J. Davis Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_J._Davis_Jr. "Benjamin J. Davis Jr.") described such reports as "exaggerated [crime wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime#public_perception "Crime") slander", and the journal _[Phylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylon "Phylon")_ wrote that conservative media aimed to "create a [Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negro "Negro") crime wave".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuddler201920%E2%80%9321-37)

### 1970s British phenomenon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mugging&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1970s British phenomenon")]

The term _mugging_ was first used in British media in the 1960s.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoran2008204-38) The media frequently reported waves of muggings from 1972 to 1976,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrakeShank19836-39) a time when the concept of [fear of crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_crime "Fear of crime") gained recognition.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJefferson2008118-40) Prior to this era, the British public had considered mugging to be limited to American cities.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawson1972306-3) Commentators of the time compared ethnic tensions in British cities to those in America, and the association of mugging with the [criminal stereotype of African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_stereotype_of_African_Americans "Criminal stereotype of African Americans") spread to Britain.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWykes2007164-9) Similar crimes in Britain had previously been called "robbery with violence", "assault and robbery", "robbery and grievous bodily harm", or "bag snatching".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeffersonClarke197437Lawson1972306-41) Such crimes had been increasingly reported starting in the mid-1960s,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELoader200145-42) and many newspapers reported police statistics saying that London's mugging rate increased 129% between 1968 and 1972.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunter201766-43) During this time, urban residents gained awareness of the risk of victimization, especially in middle-class neighborhoods whose residents had not expected crime.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTELejeuneAlex1973260%E2%80%93264-44)

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, many muggers were [West Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indian "West Indian") youths, largely due to socioeconomic discontent.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeffersonClarke197437,_48%E2%80%9349-45) Police departments strengthened [crime control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_control "Crime control") measures.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKalunta-Crumpton2000158-46) Some, including London's [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police") and [London Transport Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Transport_Police "London Transport Police"), utilized "anti-mugging" units, which primarily focused on West Indian–majority neighborhoods.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeffersonClarke197437-47) Police associated the crime with West Indians, despite high rates of mugging in some cities with low Black populations[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrakeShank19837-48) and a 1976 Metropolitan Police report to the [Home Affairs Select Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Affairs_Select_Committee "Home Affairs Select Committee") that said crime rates of West Indians were the same as the general population.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunter201766-43) Muggings received disproportionate media attention compared to other crimes that occurred in White-majority areas.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKalunta-Crumpton2000159%E2%80%93160-49) Television reports frequently featured elderly women who were victims of mugging,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerridge198390-50) and this demographic gained a widespread fear of the crime, though men were more likely to be victims.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrakeShank19837-48)

A mugging case in [Handsworth, West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsworth,_West_Midlands "Handsworth, West Midlands"), on November 5, 1972, resulted in three teenagers being sentenced to twenty years of prison and received widespread newspaper coverage.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcLaughlin2008147,_149-51) A column by commentator John Akass in _[The Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_(United\_Kingdom) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_, a widely circulated [tabloid newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabloid_journalism "Tabloid journalism"), wrote that the case's perpetrator "did not get 20 years for mugging. He got it for attempted murder," and that the punishment was "almost as barbarous as the crime itself".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcLaughlin2008150%E2%80%93151-52) The fatal stabbing of an elderly man, soon after the Handsworth case, was the first individual crime in Britain to be reported with the word _mugging_.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJefferson202140-53) Some leftist criminologists believed that the widespread attention to mugging was a result of the media rather than circumstances contributing to crime. However, [Jock Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Young "Jock Young") said in 1976, "It is unrealistic to suggest that the problem of crime like mugging is merely the problem of mis-categorization and concomitant moral panics."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcLaughlin2008147-54) In the late 1970s, public opinion largely associated mugging with Black people.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEsteves2012128-55) Politician [Enoch Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enoch_Powell "Enoch Powell") referred to mugging as a "black crime" in 1976.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKalunta-Crumpton2000158-46) A 1979 study found that two types of crime were disproportionately associated with black youths: mugging and [being suspicious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sus_law "Sus law").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPitts2020148-56)

[![Image 3: An older Black man with short, dark hair and a gray beard smiles at the camera](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8a/Hall_Stuart.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hall_Stuart.jpg)

[Stuart Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Hall_(cultural_theorist) "Stuart Hall (cultural theorist)") described mugging as a [moral panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_panic "Moral panic").

The 1978 book _[Policing the Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Policing\_the\_Crisis&action=edit&redlink=1 "Policing the Crisis (page does not exist)")_, cowritten by [Stuart Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Hall_(cultural_theorist) "Stuart Hall (cultural theorist)"), labeled the phenomenon as a [moral panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_panic "Moral panic") and argued that the media ideologically conceptualized mugging.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoran2008192,_206-57) The book said that mugging was not defined in law or distinct from existing crimes, but that the concept was influenced by preexisting societal concerns and [anti-Black sentiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_the_United_Kingdom#Black "Racism in the United Kingdom"), as well as by the connotations of the word _mugging_ in America.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoran2008203%E2%80%93204Waddington1986246%E2%80%93247-58) It argued that political and media figures used mugging to direct public fears about public disorder toward Black youths,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrayGrassoFarrallJennings2019439-59) that the government used this attitude to secure support,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrakeShank19836-39) and that media coverage of the Handsworth case exemplified the undue attention to the subject.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcLaughlin2008147-54) The book disagreed with the belief that the [crime rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_rate "Crime rate") was increasing; some critics, including Nob Doran and [P. A. J. Waddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._A._J._Waddington "P. A. J. Waddington"), said that its use of statistics was biased.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoran2008206Waddington1986248%E2%80%93250-60) Unlike Hall, Michael Pratt stated that London's rate of mugging was increasing and that the Metropolitan Police's had a legal classification equivalent to mugging.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaddington1986253%E2%80%93254-61) Colin Sumner challenged the description of mugging as a moral panic, saying that media statements did not equate to [public opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_opinion "Public opinion").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunt1997645-62)

Discussion of mugging in the [British Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Parliament "British Parliament") increased through the 1960s and 1970s (alongside that of [burglary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burglary "Burglary")) and peaked in the 1980s.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrayGrassoFarrallJennings2019444-63) By that time, [riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riot "Riot"), rather than muggings, were the subject of racialized media coverage.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunter201767-64) A survey by the [Home Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Office "Home Office"), published in March 1982, recommended [community policing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_policing "Community policing") to resist mugging and criticized excessive media response, but its findings received little attention.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerridge198390-50) Public fear of mugging peaked in the 1990s and was most prevalent among people who grew up during the era of the media phenomenon.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrayGrassoFarrallJennings2019454%E2%80%93455-65)

Brazilian media in the 1990s reported a phenomenon of mass mugging and [organized crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organized_crime "Organized crime"), termed _arrastão_ (lit.'[dragnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine_fishing "Seine fishing")').[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenglase2007306Pereira_Rosa2018188-66) The term was coined for 1992 reports of mass muggings on beaches in the wealthy [southern region of Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Zone_(Rio_de_Janeiro) "South Zone (Rio de Janeiro)"). The only injury of these incidents was caused by a police officer, and only two muggings were reported, but many people believed there was a high rate of unreported muggings. Newspapers associated the _arrastão_ with youths, particularly of the _[funkeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Funkeiro&action=edit&redlink=1 "Funkeiro (page does not exist)")_ subculture, fans of the African-American [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") music genre.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenglase2007307%E2%80%93308-67) According to anthropologist Ben Penglase, this media wave was similar to the racist reports of mugging in 1980s Britain, despite not explicitly mentioning race.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenglase2007307-68) In Portugal, a twelve-day media wave about mass mugging began after a report by [Lusa News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusa_News_Agency "Lusa News Agency") on June 10, 2005, about crime at [Carcavelos Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcavelos "Carcavelos"). Media reports used the word _arrastão_, though police said there was no evidence of it.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPereira_Rosa2018188-69) Most national news outlets and many politicians framed it as a mass mugging. Reporters gave more attention to unrelated acts, mostly by racial minorities, to support a mass mugging wave.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPereira_Rosa2018198%E2%80%93201-70)

In the 2000s, [conservatives in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatives_in_the_United_States "Conservatives in the United States") used the thesis, "A liberal is someone who has not been mugged," in support of a [law and order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_and_order_(politics) "Law and order (politics)") ideology, though being a victim of crimes such as mugging was not correlated with conservatism.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKingMaruna2009149,_161UnneverCullenFisher2007310%E2%80%93311,_322%E2%80%93326-71) American media in the late 2000s frequently reported accounts of "payday muggings", which supposed that [Mexican Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Americans "Mexican Americans"), who were thought to be likely to be [undocumented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration_to_the_United_States "Illegal immigration to the United States") and lack resources, were targeted by primarily Black muggers.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWorthamAllardLeeMortimer20119-72)

Rates of personal robbery decreased during the [COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") as there was less night-time economic activity.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEW%C3%BCllenweberBurrell20235-5)

About 2% of crimes recorded in England and Wales in the 2000s and 2010s are personal robberies.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012203-10) About one-third of personal robberies in the United Kingdom involve weapons, and about 40% of victims are injured.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012202-4) Most perpetrators in the United Kingdom are groups of young men, and most victims are men.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurrellBullBond2012203-10) In the country, fear of mugging is more prevalent among people who have been victims of it, as well as people who are women, non-white, lower-income, lower-educated, or unemployed, as of 2019.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrayGrassoFarrallJennings2019446%E2%80%93447-73)

Mugging is less frequent in Canada than the United States, as of 2005.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOuimet200590-74) In Norway, mugging is rare outside of criminal circles, but incidents are commonly reported in the media.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugging#cite_note-FOOTNOTESandbergPedersen2011128,_139-75)
